title: Era 5 Quizzes (The Nineteenth Century) — Batch 7 of 7
subtitle: Questions 1–30 · Authenticated UGC NET Stems, Keys & Explanations

items.title: Quiz Q#1501 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Which controversial novel by Thomas Hardy was serialized in Harper's New Monthly Magazine under the working titles The Simpletons and Hearts Insurgent before appearing in book form in November 1895?
items.explanation: Jude the Obscure (1895) was serialized in Harper's New Monthly Magazine as The Simpletons and Hearts Insurgent. Its bleak themes of thwarted intellectual aspiration and sexual misery provoked hostile Victorian backlash, leading Hardy to abandon novel writing for poetry.

items.title: Quiz Q#1502 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: In which Wessex novel by Thomas Hardy does the heroine Tess Durbeyfield, seduced and abandoned by Alec d'Urberville and rejected on her wedding night by Angel Clare, meet a tragic end at Stonehenge?
items.explanation: Tess Durbeyfield is the tragic protagonist of Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891). Hardy depicts her as a victim of social hypocrisy, aristocratic decay, and unyielding fate.

items.title: Quiz Q#1503 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Who is the author of the Wessex novel that concludes with the famous philosophical verdict: "'Justice' was done, and the President of the Immortals, in Aeschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess"?
items.explanation: This famous closing judgment appears in Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), reflecting Hardy's fatalistic view of cosmic indifference toward human suffering.

items.title: Quiz Q#1504 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Serialized in a heavily censored form in The Graphic in 1891, which Thomas Hardy novel challenged Victorian moral orthodoxies with its defiant subtitle, 'A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented'?
items.explanation: Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented (1891) was serialized in The Graphic after several editors rejected it. Hardy's subtitle deliberately defended Tess's essential moral purity against rigid Victorian conventions.

items.title: Quiz Q#1505 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: In which novel by Thomas Hardy does Michael Henchard, an impulsive hay-trusser who drunkenly sells his wife and infant daughter at Weydon-Priors fair, rise to become a prosperous corn merchant and chief civic magistrate?
items.explanation: Michael Henchard is the tragic protagonist of Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886). The novel traces how Henchard's past misdeed and volatile temper bring about his downfall in rivalry with Donald Farfrae.

items.title: Quiz Q#1506 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Which Victorian novelist concludes his tragic study of Michael Henchard with Elizabeth-Jane's somber reflection that "happiness was but the occasional episode in a general drama of pain"?
items.explanation: This poignant concluding line appears in Thomas Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), encapsulating Hardy's tragic worldview and Elizabeth-Jane's mature stoicism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1507 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Subtitled 'The Life and Death of a Man of Character', which Thomas Hardy novel serialized in The Graphic in 1886 dramatizes the rivalry between Michael Henchard and Donald Farfrae?
items.explanation: The Mayor of Casterbridge: The Life and Death of a Man of Character was serialized in The Graphic from January to May 1886. Hardy drew inspiration from Novalis's aphorism that 'Character is Fate.'

items.title: Quiz Q#1508 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · J. M. Synge
items.stem: In which Irish play by J. M. Synge does Christy Mahon, a timid youth who arrives at a Mayo village tavern boasting that he has killed his tyrannical father with a loy, become a celebrated local hero?
options: The Playboy of the Western World
items.explanation: Christy Mahon is the central protagonist of J. M. Synge's comic masterpiece The Playboy of the Western World (1907). The play satirizes romanticized violence and community myth-making.

items.title: Quiz Q#1509 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · J. M. Synge
items.stem: Who is the Irish dramatist of the play that concludes with Pegeen Mike's heartbroken cry: "Oh my grief, I've lost him surely. I've lost the only Playboy of the Western World"?
items.explanation: This iconic closing line is spoken by Pegeen Mike at the end of J. M. Synge's The Playboy of the Western World (1907), following Christy Mahon's departure with his father.

items.title: Quiz Q#1510 · J. M. Synge
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · J. M. Synge
items.stem: Which landmark Irish drama, premiered at Dublin's Abbey Theatre in January 1907, incited public rioting over its realistic depiction of peasant morality and the onstage mention of a woman's undergarment ('shift')?
options: The Playboy of the Western World
items.explanation: The Playboy of the Western World (1907) sparked the famous 'Playboy Riots' at the Abbey Theatre. Irish nationalist audiences protested against Synge's perceived slander of Irish womanhood and peasant culture.

items.title: Quiz Q#1511 · James Joyce
items.stem: In which work by James Joyce does Gabriel Conroy experience a paralyzing spiritual epiphany while watching snow fall softly across Ireland, after his wife Gretta recalls her lost love Michael Furey?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: Gabriel Conroy is the central figure in 'The Dead', the culminating story of James Joyce's Dubliners (1914). His self-absorbed complacency shatters into profound emotional awareness of mortality and love.

items.title: Quiz Q#1512 · James Joyce
items.stem: Who is the Irish modernist author whose celebrated short story 'The Dead' concludes with the lyrical cadence: "snow was general all over Ireland"?
items.explanation: This celebrated final passage appears in James Joyce's 'The Dead', the final masterpiece in Dubliners (1914), symbolizing death and spiritual paralysis blanketing the living and the dead.

items.title: Quiz Q#1513 · James Joyce
items.stem: Which landmark short story collection by James Joyce was begun in 1904 for The Irish Homestead under the pseudonym 'Stephen Daedalus', exploring the paralyzing moral, political, and spiritual stagnation of Irish city life?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: Dubliners (1914) is Joyce's collection of fifteen naturalistic stories progressing through childhood, adolescence, mature life, and public life, all united by the central motif of paralysis.

items.title: Quiz Q#1514 · James Joyce
items.stem: In which semi-autobiographical bildungsroman by James Joyce does Stephen Dedalus reject Catholic dogma and Irish nationalism in order to "forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race"?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: Stephen Dedalus is the protagonist of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916). The novel traces his intellectual, aesthetic, and spiritual development through distinct linguistic stages.

items.title: Quiz Q#1515 · James Joyce
items.stem: Completely rewritten and condensed from the discarded naturalistic manuscript Stephen Hero, which modernist masterpiece by James Joyce was serialized in The Egoist between 1914 and 1915?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was serialized in Harriet Shaw Weaver and Ezra Pound's journal The Egoist (1914–1915). Joyce discarded the sprawling Stephen Hero in favor of a tightly focused mythic structure.

items.title: Quiz Q#1516 · James Joyce
items.stem: In which monumental modernist novel by James Joyce does Leopold Bloom wander through the streets, pubs, and cemeteries of Dublin on 16 June 1904 as a modern everyday counterpart to Odysseus?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: Leopold Bloom is the humane, observant protagonist of Joyce's Ulysses (1922). The novel reconstructs the 18 episodes of Homer's Odyssey across Dublin on a single day, now celebrated as Bloomsday.

items.title: Quiz Q#1517 · James Joyce
items.stem: Which modernist author opens his landmark novel with the famous line: "Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed"?
items.explanation: This famous opening sentence begins the 'Telemachus' episode of James Joyce's Ulysses (1922), set at the Martello tower in Sandycove, Dublin.

items.title: Quiz Q#1518 · James Joyce
items.stem: Serialized in the American avant-garde magazine The Little Review from 1918 until it was prosecuted for obscenity, which landmark modernist novel was first published in book form in Paris by Sylvia Beach in 1922?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: Joyce's Ulysses was serialized in The Little Review before being seized and banned in the US. Sylvia Beach published the complete first edition under her Shakespeare and Company imprint in Paris on 2 February 1922.

items.title: Quiz Q#1519 · James Joyce
items.stem: In which linguistically radical work by James Joyce does the Dublin publican Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker (HCE), along with his wife Anna Livia Plurabelle (ALP), form the mythic archetype dreaming through cyclical human history?
options: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
items.explanation: Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker (HCE, 'Here Comes Everybody') is the central dreaming figure in Finnegans Wake (1939). Joyce uses a polyglot dream-language structured around Giambattista Vico's cyclical philosophy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1520 · James Joyce
items.stem: Who is the modernist author whose final, monumental night-world book begins mid-sentence with the words: "riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, from swerve of shore to bend of bay, brings us by a commodius vicus of recirculation..."?
items.explanation: This celebrated opening line begins James Joyce's Finnegans Wake (1939). The novel's closing broken sentence cycles directly back into this opening clause, embodying eternal recurrence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1521 · James Joyce
items.stem: Known during its seventeen-year composition simply as 'Work in Progress' and published in serial excerpts in Eugene Jolas's journal transition, which final work by James Joyce was published in 1939?
items.explanation: Finnegans Wake (1939) occupied Joyce from 1923 to 1939 under the working title Work in Progress. He kept its true title a secret until shortly before Faber and Faber and Viking Press published it simultaneously.

items.title: Quiz Q#1522 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: In which villanelle by Dylan Thomas does the speaker passionately exhort his dying, blind father to "Rage, rage against the dying of the light" rather than surrender peacefully to death?
options: And death shall have no dominion
Do not go gentle into that good night
items.explanation: Dylan Thomas wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night' (1951) for his ailing father, D. J. Thomas. The poem employs the rigorous 19-line villanelle form with two alternating refrains.

items.title: Quiz Q#1523 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Who is the Welsh poet who composed the celebrated villanelle opening with the lines: "Do not go gentle into that good night, / Old age should burn and rave at close of day; / Rage, rage against the dying of the light"?
items.explanation: Dylan Thomas composed this famous villanelle in 1951, presenting four categories of men (wise men, good men, wild men, and grave men) who defy mortality before addressing his father directly.

items.title: Quiz Q#1524 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: First printed in the Italian literary journal Botteghe Oscure in 1951 before appearing in In Country Sleep, which strict 19-line villanelle by Dylan Thomas meditates fiercely on filial devotion and mortality?
options: And death shall have no dominion
A Refusal to Mourn the Death, by Fire, of a Child in London
Do not go gentle into that good night
items.explanation: 'Do not go gentle into that good night' was first published in Florence in Botteghe Oscure (1951) and collected in In Country Sleep (1952). It remains one of the most famous villanelles in English literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1525 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Which 1934 debut collection launched the literary career of twenty-year-old Dylan Thomas, containing iconic surrealist lyrics such as 'The force that through the green fuse drives the flower'?
items.explanation: 18 Poems (December 1934) was Dylan Thomas's astonishing debut, published jointly by the Sunday Referee and the Parton Bookshop. It introduced his distinctive metaphysical imagery of birth, sex, and death.

items.title: Quiz Q#1526 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Which 20th-century poet wrote the visionary lyric anchored by the biblical refrain from St. Paul's Epistle to the Romans: "And death shall have no dominion"?
items.explanation: Dylan Thomas published 'And death shall have no dominion' in 1933 in the New English Weekly, later collected in Twenty-five Poems (1936), proclaiming spiritual transcendence over physical mortality.

items.title: Quiz Q#1527 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Published in 1936 by J. M. Dent, which second poetry collection by Dylan Thomas established his major reputation and included 'And death shall have no dominion' and the sonnet sequence 'Altarwise by owl-light'?
items.explanation: Twenty-five Poems (1936) confirmed Dylan Thomas's status as a major lyric poet of the New Apocalypse generation, celebrated for its verbal density and the complex sonnets of 'Altarwise by owl-light.'

items.title: Quiz Q#1528 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Which 1946 poetry collection by Dylan Thomas, written during the London Blitz and World War II, includes his famous nostalgic pastoral 'Fern Hill' and the elegy 'A Refusal to Mourn the Death, by Fire, of a Child in London'?
items.explanation: Deaths and Entrances (1946) is regarded as Dylan Thomas's finest single volume of verse, marked by heightened religious symbolism and celebrated lyrics such as 'Fern Hill' and 'Poem in October.'

items.title: Quiz Q#1529 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: In which radio play ('a play for voices') by Dylan Thomas does the omniscient First Voice guide listeners through the nocturnal dreams and waking gossip of the fictional Welsh fishing village Llareggub?
options: Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog
items.explanation: The First Voice is the lyrical narrator in Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood (1954), providing an intimate, richly textured auditory portrait of Llareggub's eccentric inhabitants.

items.title: Quiz Q#1530 · Dylan Thomas
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Play for Voices' and set in the fictional Welsh seaside village of Llareggub, which celebrated radio drama by Dylan Thomas was broadcast posthumously by the BBC Third Programme in 1954 starring Richard Burton?
options: Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog
items.explanation: Under Milk Wood: A Play for Voices was commissioned by the BBC and completed just before Thomas's death in New York in 1953. Its legendary BBC broadcast in January 1954 starred Richard Burton as First Voice.
